versions.request: Renovate, upgrade or provide new community board facilities and equipment
versions.explanation: BKCB2 recommends a comprehensive assessment of our operating and technical needs, and a commensurate increase in our baseline operating budget. There has been no Citywide assessment of Community Board technical needs since Windstream acquired PAETEC's municipal contracts in 2011. Windstream has consistently failed to provide reliable phone and internet service or equipment since beginning bankruptcy proceedings in 2019. This is just one example of widespread underinvestment in the basic needs of Community Board operations. A recurring theme expressed by our City agency partners across all of this year's Borough Budget Consultations was, ""We are budgeted to address [X program/concern], but we need more support with direct local outreach."" The general public is also increasingly expectant that government offices utilize modern tools and offer digital connectivity. As the most local unit of nonpartisan City government, Community Boards need an infusion of infrastructure, equipment, and staff support to meet modern challenges, effectively partner with City agencies, efficiently serve our residents, and support greater community engagement. The scope of assessment and investment must include basic office and field equipment updates; a survey of phone, internet, and broadcasting infrastructure and gaps; a survey of staff training and upskilling needs; and baselining of fundamental SaaS tools including design and communication (newsletter) software, and news, database, and research subscriptions. To be clear, this requires a significant periodic investment above our extremely modest $13-$15k average annual OTPS allotment. We recommend commitment to a 4-year cycle of regular operational and technical assessments and upgrades.

versions.request: Other capital budget request for DOHMH
versions.explanation: BKCB2 recommends increased DOHMH funding in BKCD2 for street-level air quality monitors through the NYC Community Air Survey (NYCCAS) program, and exploration of collaboration opportunities with our State DEC partners to implement rooftop monitors on our NYCHA campuses and the Manhattan and Brooklyn Bridges. Particulate matter that is 2.5m or smaller (""PM2.5"") penetrates deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing chronic and often lethal heart and lung disease. Internal Combustion Engines (ICE) such as gas-powered vehicles are the leading source of PM2.5. Long term exposure to PM2.5 contributes to 1 out of 25 deaths in NYC, and per the 2018 Community Health Profile, the levels of fine particulate matter and the rate of child asthma emergency room visits are notably higher in BKCD2 than in NYC as a whole. BKCD2 contains 1.5 miles (12%) of the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway (BQE) within its boundaries and has 3 Neighborhood Tabulation Areas in Brooklyn's 10 highest PM2.5 levels--the most of any Brooklyn Community District. This request is particularly urgent given the Trump Administration's recent reversal of the Biden Administration's EPA limits on PM2.5.
versions.response: The agency will try to accommodate this issue within existing resources. OMB supports the agency's position.

versions.request: Increase enforcement of street vending
versions.explanation: BKCB2 recommends funding for a feasibility study regarding creation of a mulit-agency task force to reduce unauthorized and non-compliant street vendors. versions.explanation: BKCB2 requests a baselined annual budget increase of $26,160 to send an annual direct mailer to the ~80,000 households in BKCD2 to inform them of the City Charter-mandated municipal information, resident assistance, and civic participation opportunities available to them through their Community Board and District Office. Printing: $0.08/postcard = $6,400 USPS EDDM bulk postage: $0.247/postcard = $19,760 Investing in Community Boards is an investment in accountable, equitable, and responsive government for every New Yorker. Community Boards play a uniquely democratic role in shaping development, addressing neighborhood concerns, ensuring residents have a voice in city decisions, and educating residents about municipal systems and functions. Yet we operate with one third of the staff of City Council offices despite serving a similar-sized population, and are typically allocated an OTPS budget of less than $15k per year. Increasing our baseline budget specifically for outreach purposes would strengthen our ability to reach and engage the public, conduct meaningful planning, and respond effectively to community needs. Outreach will become even more urgent in the coming decade as Community Board term limits take effect, thereby decreasing institutional knowledge and increasing the need for new Member recruitment.
versions.response: As of the FY 2027 Executive Budget, each Community Board's budget is being maintained.
